absolute-majority.label: Absolute Majority
absolute-majority.popup: A majority of a chamber's full seated membership — counted against every seat filled, not just the members present or voting.
absolute-majority.detail: The standard threshold for passing legislation under §3.7, and the bar for removing a Civic Consul under §2.6's constructive vote of no confidence. Counting against full membership rather than attendance means a thin turnout cannot lower the bar — abstaining or being absent has the same practical effect as voting no.

dual-executive.label: Dual Executive
dual-executive.popup: Two separately selected executives with enumerated, non-overlapping domains — neither one is head of government alone.
dual-executive.detail: The Legat Consul (§2.1) holds military command, foreign affairs, and external intelligence. The Civic Consul (§2.5) holds residual authority over everything else. They are selected differently, removed differently, and neither can act in the other's domain. The Council of Ministers (§2.14) is where their domains coordinate — it recommends and aligns positions, but exercises no executive authority of its own.

classification-ceiling.label: Classification Ceiling
classification-ceiling.popup: 25 years maximum, extendable once by five — and never past 30 under any circumstances.
classification-ceiling.detail: On expiry the NRS Panel publishes the record automatically, with no government act required. The single 5-year extension requires the responsible executive to publish a justification, which the EM assesses and reports on — though that finding binds no one. Any person with standing may petition at any time for release: the court orders release of every portion whose disclosure would not itself satisfy the statutory ground for classification, and publishes the redactions and the ground for each.

officer-removal.label: Constitutional Officer Removal
officer-removal.popup: Two separate tracks: Monitor Generals are removed by national referendum, other independent officers within §9.9’s scope by a two-thirds vote of both chambers.
officer-removal.detail: For Monitor Generals, removal is initiated by the branch that Monitor does not audit — for the Executive Monitor, the Legislature by concurrent resolution — and completed only by a national referendum at 60% of votes cast with 55% participation. Filing does not suspend the Monitor General, and a failed referendum bars the same grounds for the rest of the term. For other independent officers within §9.9’s scope, one-third of either chamber or two Monitor Generals may initiate, and removal requires a concurrent two-thirds vote of each chamber on statutory grounds.

electoral-mandate-inviolability.label: Inviolability of Electoral Mandates
electoral-mandate-inviolability.popup: An elected officer serves their full term — no branch, court, Monitor, or agency can cut it short outside the paths this Constitution names.
electoral-mandate-inviolability.detail: The only exceptions are chamber expulsion, State-law recall, and removal mechanisms expressly provided by the Constitution, subject to §7.5. Creating any new way for the people to shorten a mandate requires a constitutional amendment, not a statute. Expulsion, recall, and removal are political processes rather than legal ones — they end an officer's tenure without shielding them from criminal prosecution or civil liability for the underlying conduct.

constructive-vote-no-confidence.label: Constructive Vote of No Confidence
constructive-vote-no-confidence.popup: The Assembly can only remove a Civic Consul by naming their replacement in the same vote.
constructive-vote-no-confidence.detail: A confidence vote that does not name a successor has no effect. This makes removal an act of choosing a different government rather than simply ending the current one — the office never falls vacant, and a coalition that can agree on removal but not on a replacement cannot force a crisis.
